q: Operating (service) costing is essentially:

options.A: Job costing applied to service undertakings
options.B: Process costing applied to undertakings which provide services instead of manufacturing goods
options.C: Batch costing applied to transport undertakings

e: Operating costing is essentially process costing applied to undertakings which provide services instead of manufacturing goods, the cost being ascertained per unit of service rendered.

q: A transport undertaking incurs a total operating cost of Rs 15,00,000 during a period in which its vehicles run 2,50,000 kilometres. The operating cost per vehicle-kilometre is:
e: Operating cost per vehicle-kilometre = total operating cost / kilometres run = 15,00,000 / 2,50,000 = Rs 6.

q: A power house incurs total operating costs of Rs 24,00,000 during a period in which it generates 12,00,000 kWh of electricity. The cost per kWh generated is:
e: Cost per kWh generated = total operating cost / units generated = 24,00,000 / 12,00,000 = Rs 2.

q: In activity-based costing, a 'cost driver' is:

options.A: The head of a cost centre
options.B: A machine which consumes the maximum power
options.C: The total amount of an activity cost pool
options.D: A factor which causes a change in the cost of an activity and on the basis of which activity costs are assigned to cost objects

e: A cost driver is a factor which causes a change in the cost of an activity; under ABC, activity costs are assigned to cost objects on the basis of the cost drivers they consume.

q: Under activity-based costing, the procurement (buying) cost pool of a factory is Rs 2,40,000 and the total number of purchase orders placed in the period is 800. A product for which 120 purchase orders were placed will be assigned procurement cost of:
e: Rate per purchase order = 2,40,000 / 800 = Rs 300; procurement cost assigned = 120 orders x 300 = Rs 36,000.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 3,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 1,50,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 3 years at 12% is 2.402. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: NPV = present value of inflows - initial outlay = (1,50,000 x 2.402) - 3,00,000 = 3,60,300 - 3,00,000 = (+) Rs 60,300.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 6,00,000. Its net cash inflows are Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 12% = 0.893), Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 12% = 0.797) and Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor at 12% = 0.712). The Net Present Value of the project is:

A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 3,50,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 80,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 8% is 3.993. The Net Present Value of the project is:
The present value of Rs 4,00,000 receivable at the end of 4 years, discounted at 10% (present value factor 0.683), is:
e: Present value = future amount x present value factor = 4,00,000 x 0.683 = Rs 2,73,200.

q: Rs 50,000 invested today at 10% per annum compound interest will grow in 2 years to:
e: Future value = 50,000 x (1.10)^2 = 50,000 x 1.21 = Rs 60,500, interest being compounded for the second year on the principal plus first year's interest.

q: A machine costing Rs 4,80,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 1,60,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: Payback period = initial cost / annual net cash inflow = 4,80,000 / 1,60,000 = 3 years.

q: A project costing Rs 6,50,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,50,000 in Year 1, Rs 2,50,000 in Year 2, Rs 2,00,000 in Year 3 and Rs 2,00,000 in Year 4. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,50,000, Year 2 Rs 4,00,000, Year 3 Rs 6,00,000; the balance of Rs 50,000 is recovered in 3 months of Year 4 (50,000 / 2,00,000 x 12), so payback = 3 years 3 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 3,60,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,20,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 1,20,000 at the end of Year 2, Rs 90,000 at the end of Year 3 and Rs 60,000 at the end of Year 4. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Cumulative present value by end of Year 3 = 1,20,000 + 1,20,000 + 90,000 = Rs 3,30,000; the balance of Rs 30,000 is half of Year 4's Rs 60,000, so discounted payback = 3 years 6 months.

q: A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 10,000 at a discount rate of 11% and (-) Rs 5,000 at a discount rate of 14%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: By interpolation, IRR = 11% + (10,000 / (10,000 + 5,000)) x (14% - 11%) = 11% + 2% = 13%, the rate at which the NPV becomes zero.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 5,20,000 and its initial investment is Rs 4,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = present value of future cash inflows / initial investment = 5,20,000 / 4,00,000 = 1.30.

q: An investment of Rs 18,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 1,98,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: Average Rate of Return = average annual profit / initial investment x 100 = 1,98,000 / 18,00,000 x 100 = 11%.

q: An investment of Rs 9,00,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 3,00,000 at the end of its life, so that the average investment over its life is Rs 6,00,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 72,000, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
e: ARR on average investment = average annual profit / average investment x 100 = 72,000 / 6,00,000 x 100 = 12%.

q: In appraising a project whose cash flows are expressed in nominal (current-price) terms, the discount rate to be used is:

options.A: The real rate of discount, so that inflation is excluded twice
options.B: The nominal (money) rate of discount, which includes an allowance for inflation

e: Cash flows expressed in nominal (current-price) terms include inflation, so they must be discounted at the nominal (money) rate of discount, which also includes an allowance for inflation; mixing a real rate with nominal flows would distort the result.

q: A company's capital structure consists of debt of Rs 5,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 8% and equity of Rs 15,00,000 with a cost of 14%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:

A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 12,00,000 (cost 13%), preference capital of Rs 3,00,000 (cost 10%) and debt of Rs 5,00,000 (after-tax cost 6%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues 11% debentures at par. If the tax rate is 30%, the after-tax cost of debt is:
e: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, so the after-tax cost of debt = 11% x (1 - 0.30) = 7.7%.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 12 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 120 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 5% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity under the dividend growth model = (expected dividend / market price) + growth rate = (12 / 120) + 5% = 10% + 5% = 15%.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 9%, the expected market return is 16% and the beta of the share is 0.9, the cost of equity is:
e: Under CAPM, cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate) = 9% + 0.9 x (16% - 9%) = 9% + 6.3% = 15.3%.

q: The 'specific cost of capital' of an enterprise refers to:

options.A: The cost of a particular source of finance, such as the cost of equity or the cost of debt, taken by itself
options.B: The combined cost of all sources of finance taken together
options.C: The cost of capital of a specific project division only
options.D: The historical cost of the capital already raised

e: Specific cost of capital is the cost of a particular source of finance taken by itself, such as the cost of equity or the cost of debt; the weighted average of all sources is the combined cost.

q: The cost of capital of an enterprise is best described as:

options.A: The dividend rate declared in the previous year
options.B: The interest rate charged by its bankers on working capital loans
options.C: The average of the interest rates on all its borrowings
options.D: The minimum rate of return which the enterprise must earn on its investments in order to maintain (leave unchanged) its market value

e: The cost of capital is the minimum rate of return the enterprise must earn on its investments in order to maintain (leave unchanged) its market value; earning less than this rate reduces the value of the firm.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000, variable costs are Rs 7,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 2,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 10,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 3,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - interest) = 10,00,000 / (10,00,000 - 3,00,000) = 10,00,000 / 7,00,000 = 1.43.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 15,00,000, variable costs of Rs 8,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 3,00,000 and interest of Rs 1,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Degree of combined leverage = contribution / (contribution - fixed costs - interest) = 7,00,000 / (7,00,000 - 3,00,000 - 1,00,000) = 7,00,000 / 3,00,000 = 2.33.

q: The degree of combined leverage of an enterprise is 2.5. If its sales increase by 12%, its Earnings Per Share will increase by approximately:
e: Percentage increase in EPS = degree of combined leverage x percentage increase in sales = 2.5 x 12% = 30%.

q: An enterprise is financed entirely by equity capital and has no debt at all. Its degree of financial leverage will be:

options.B: One (unity), since there is no interest burden to magnify the effect of changes in EBIT on the earnings of equity holders
options.D: Equal to its degree of operating leverage

e: With no debt there is no interest burden, so changes in EBIT pass to the equity holders without magnification and the degree of financial leverage is one (unity).

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 13,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 5,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = 13,00,000 / 5,00,000 = 2.6 : 1.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 7,20,000, including stock of Rs 2,40,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 30,000. Current liabilities are Rs 1,50,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = 7,20,000 - stock 2,40,000 - prepaid expenses 30,000 = Rs 4,50,000; quick ratio = 4,50,000 / 1,50,000 = 3 : 1.

q: Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 6,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 8,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = long-term debt / shareholders' funds = 6,00,000 / 8,00,000 = 0.75 : 1.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 24,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 15,00,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 75,000 on sales of Rs 6,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = net profit / sales x 100 = 75,000 / 6,00,000 x 100 = 12.5%.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 11,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 1,00,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
e: Inventory turnover ratio = cost of goods sold / average inventory = 11,00,000 / 1,00,000 = 11 times.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 16,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,60,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = credit sales / average debtors = 16,00,000 / 1,60,000 = 10 times.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 13,00,000 and the interest payable is Rs 2,00,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = profit before interest and tax / interest = 13,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 6.5 times.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 3,15,000 and its capital employed is Rs 9,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: Return on Capital Employed = profit before interest and tax / capital employed x 100 = 3,15,000 / 9,00,000 x 100 = 35%.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 7,50,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 1,50,000. If the company has 80,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (net profit after tax - preference dividend) / number of equity shares = (7,50,000 - 1,50,000) / 80,000 = 6,00,000 / 80,000 = Rs 7.50 per share.

q: Ratio analysis is useful to the management of an enterprise mainly because it:

options.B: Guarantees the future profits of the enterprise
options.C: Eliminates the need for auditing the accounts
options.D: Simplifies and summarises the accounting data and facilitates comparison - between firms, and of the same firm over a period of time

e: Ratio analysis simplifies and summarises the accounting data into meaningful relationships and facilitates comparison - between firms, and of the same firm over a period of time - which is its main use to management.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 2,00,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 35,000 and a loss of Rs 8,000 on the sale of furniture, and after crediting a profit of Rs 18,000 on the sale of land. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = 2,00,000 + 35,000 (depreciation) + 8,000 (loss on sale of furniture) - 18,000 (profit on sale of land) = Rs 2,25,000; non-cash charges are added back and non-operating credits deducted.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 3,20,000. During the year, its stock increased by Rs 25,000, its debtors decreased by Rs 40,000 and its creditors decreased by Rs 20,000. The cash from operations is:
e: Cash from operations = 3,20,000 - 25,000 (stock increase blocks cash) + 40,000 (debtors decrease releases cash) - 20,000 (creditors decrease uses cash) = Rs 3,15,000.

q: During a year, the current assets of an enterprise decreased by Rs 60,000 and its current liabilities increased by Rs 40,000. The net change in its working capital is:
e: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities; a decrease of Rs 60,000 in current assets together with an increase of Rs 40,000 in current liabilities reduces working capital by Rs 1,00,000.

q: In a cash flow statement prepared under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the cash proceeds received on the issue of debentures are classified as:

options.C: Not shown in the cash flow statement

e: Under AS-3, the cash proceeds received on the issue of debentures are borrowings raised by the enterprise and are therefore classified as a financing activity.

q: A railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 2,00,000 crore against ordinary working expenses of Rs 1,76,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = ordinary working expenses / gross traffic receipts x 100 = 1,76,000 / 2,00,000 x 100 = 88%.

q: The net earnings of a railway are Rs 10,500 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 1,50,000 crore. The return on capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = net earnings / capital-at-charge x 100 = 10,500 / 1,50,000 x 100 = 7%.

q: A proposed railway work is estimated to cost Rs 400 crore and is expected to yield net annual earnings of Rs 46 crore after meeting the additional working expenses. The anticipated rate of return on the work, and its financial status, are:

options.A: 10%; the work just meets the prescribed test
options.D: 11.5%; the work is remunerative, as it exceeds the prescribed 10% test

e: Rate of return = 46 / 400 x 100 = 11.5%. Since 11.5% exceeds the prescribed 10% test of remunerativeness, the work is remunerative, i.e. financially justified.

q: The financial justification of major railway works such as new lines is generally prepared by applying:

options.A: The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) technique, in which the anticipated earnings and costs over the life of the work are discounted to their present value
options.C: The average rate of return method alone
options.D: A simple comparison of the first year's earnings with the capital cost

e: The financial justification of major railway works is generally prepared by applying the Discounted Cash Flow technique, in which the anticipated earnings and costs over the life of the work are discounted to their present value.

q: An Operating Ratio of more than 100% for a railway indicates that:

options.A: The railway's earnings exceed its working expenses
options.B: The ordinary working expenses of the railway exceed its gross traffic earnings, i.e., the railway is incurring an operating deficit
options.C: The capital-at-charge has been fully repaid
options.D: The railway requires no budgetary support

e: An Operating Ratio of more than 100% means the ordinary working expenses exceed the gross traffic earnings, so the railway is incurring an operating deficit and its earnings do not cover its working expenses.

q: The standard hours required for the actual output of a department are 9,350 hours and the budgeted hours for the department are 11,000 hours. The activity ratio of the department is:
e: Activity ratio = Standard hours for actual output / Budgeted hours x 100 = 9,350 / 11,000 x 100 = 85%. It measures the level of activity actually achieved against the budgeted level.

q: The master budget of an enterprise, prepared by consolidating all the functional budgets, becomes operative only after it has been approved by:

options.A: The statutory auditor of the enterprise
options.B: The Board of Directors or the top management of the enterprise
options.D: The shareholders in the annual general meeting

e: The master budget is the summary budget consolidating all functional budgets. It becomes operative only after approval by the Board of Directors or top management, who alone can commit the enterprise to the plan.

q: In a manufacturing enterprise in which sales demand is the principal budget factor, the functional budget which is generally prepared first, and from which the preparation of the other budgets proceeds, is the:
e: Where sales demand is the principal budget factor, the sales budget is prepared first because production, purchases, labour and cash budgets all depend on the expected volume and value of sales.

q: The budgeted cash sales of an enterprise for March are Rs 60,000. Debtors outstanding at the beginning of March are Rs 1,50,000, the whole of which is expected to be collected during March. Credit sales to be made during March are Rs 1,80,000, but these will be collected only in April. The total cash receipts budgeted for March are:
e: March receipts = cash sales Rs 60,000 + opening debtors collected Rs 1,50,000 = Rs 2,10,000. The March credit sales of Rs 1,80,000 are collected only in April, so they are excluded.

q: Production of 22,000 units is budgeted. Each unit requires 3 kg of material, the price of which is Rs 6 per kg. The materials usage (consumption) budget for the period will be:
e: Materials usage budget = production units x material per unit x price = 22,000 x 3 kg x Rs 6 = Rs 3,96,000. It covers consumption in production, not purchases.

q: A production budget provides for 8,000 units. Each unit requires 2.5 standard labour hours and the standard wage rate is Rs 30 per hour. The direct labour cost budget will be:
e: Direct labour cost budget = units x standard hours per unit x wage rate = 8,000 x 2.5 hours x Rs 30 = Rs 6,00,000.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 40 days, the production process takes 25 days, finished goods are held for 20 days and debtors take 60 days to pay. Suppliers allow 35 days' credit. The length of the operating cycle is:
e: Operating cycle = raw material holding 40 + production 25 + finished goods 20 + debtors 60 - creditors 35 = 110 days.

q: The estimated annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 21,60,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 45 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = annual operating cost / 360 x cycle days = Rs 21,60,000 / 360 x 45 = Rs 6,000 x 45 = Rs 2,70,000.

q: An enterprise has an inventory conversion period of 80 days, a receivables collection period of 35 days and a payables deferral period of 45 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:
e: Cash conversion cycle = inventory period + receivables period - payables period = 80 + 35 - 45 = 70 days, the time cash stays locked in operations.

q: The current liabilities of an enterprise are Rs 2,75,000 and its net working capital is Rs 5,25,000. Its current assets are:
e: Current assets = net working capital + current liabilities = Rs 5,25,000 + Rs 2,75,000 = Rs 8,00,000, since net working capital is current assets minus current liabilities.

q: An enterprise which is working with inadequate (deficient) working capital is likely to face:

options.A: Large idle cash balances lying unutilised
options.D: Inability to pay its creditors on time and loss of cash discounts, with a constant strain on liquidity, even though the business itself may be profitable

e: Deficient working capital means current assets barely cover or fall short of current liabilities, so creditors cannot be paid on time, cash discounts are lost and liquidity stays strained even in a profitable business.

q: Under the regression analysis method of estimating working capital:

options.A: Every component of working capital is taken as a fixed percentage of the sales
options.B: The statistical relationship between sales and working capital (and its components) is established from past data by the least-squares method and applied to the forecast level of sales
options.C: The estimate is prepared only by the bankers of the enterprise
options.D: Only the cash component of working capital is forecast

e: The regression method uses least-squares on past data to establish how working capital and each component vary with sales, then applies that statistical relationship to the forecast sales level.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 380 units per week and the maximum re-order period is 5 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:
e: Re-order level = maximum consumption x maximum re-order period = 380 units x 5 weeks = 1,900 units, the level at which a fresh order must be placed.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,900 units. Normal consumption is 220 units per week and the normal re-order period is 6 weeks. The minimum stock level is:
e: Minimum stock level = re-order level - (normal consumption x normal re-order period) = 2,900 - (220 x 6) = 2,900 - 1,320 = 1,580 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,100 units and the re-order quantity is 1,300 units. Minimum consumption is 110 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 4 weeks. The maximum stock level is:
e: Maximum stock level = re-order level + re-order quantity - (minimum consumption x minimum re-order period) = 2,100 + 1,300 - (110 x 4) = 2,960 units.

q: The minimum stock level of a material is 650 units and the re-order quantity is 1,500 units. The average stock level is:
e: Average stock level = minimum level + half the re-order quantity = 650 + (1,500 / 2) = 650 + 750 = 1,400 units.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 650 units per week, the normal consumption is 400 units per week and the maximum lead time is 4 weeks. The safety stock, computed as (Maximum consumption - Normal consumption) x Maximum lead time, is:
e: Safety stock = (maximum consumption - normal consumption) x maximum lead time = (650 - 400) x 4 = 250 x 4 = 1,000 units, held as a buffer against delays and surges.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 7,200 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 45 and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 7,200 x 45 / 5) = sqrt(1,29,600) = 360 units, the order size where total ordering cost equals total carrying cost.

q: Materials Requirement Planning (MRP) is a system under which:

options.A: The quantities and timings of materials and components required are worked out from the production schedule (master production plan), the bill of materials of each product and the inventory records, so that materials arrive just as they are needed for production
options.B: Materials are purchased in bulk at the beginning of every year on the basis of the previous year's consumption
options.C: The storekeeper places an order whenever he finds a bin empty, without reference to the production programme
options.D: Materials are issued to production only against cash payment by the production departments

e: MRP explodes the master production schedule through the bill of materials, netting off inventory records, to work out what materials and components are needed, in what quantity and by when.

q: The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 36,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 2,40,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = average debtors / credit sales x 360 = Rs 2,40,000 / Rs 36,00,000 x 360 = 24 days.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 30,80,000 and its average debtors are Rs 2,20,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = credit sales / average debtors = Rs 30,80,000 / Rs 2,20,000 = 14 times, showing how often receivables are collected in the year.

q: A steadily shortening average payment period of an enterprise, other things remaining the same, generally indicates that:

options.A: The credit management of the enterprise has become lax
options.B: The enterprise has stopped purchasing goods altogether
options.C: The suppliers have refused to sell goods to the enterprise
options.D: The enterprise is paying its suppliers promptly — possibly in order to earn cash discounts — and is not availing itself of the full period of trade credit available to it

e: A shortening payment period means suppliers are being paid sooner than the credit allowed, possibly to earn cash discounts; the firm is not using the full interest-free trade credit available.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 4/10, net 40. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of forgoing discount = (4 / 96) x (360 / (40 - 10)) = 0.0417 x 12 = 50% per annum, the effective yearly cost of paying on day 40 instead of day 10.

q: The main purpose of offering a cash discount to customers is to:

options.A: Increase the list price of the goods sold
options.B: Reduce the quality specifications of the goods
options.C: Induce the customers to pay their dues promptly, thereby accelerating collections and reducing the funds blocked in receivables
options.D: Avoid the payment of tax on the sales

e: A cash discount rewards early payment, so customers settle promptly; collections accelerate, funds blocked in receivables fall, and bad-debt risk and collection effort are reduced.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 32,00,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 25 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 10% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Optimum cash balance = sqrt(2AT / i) = sqrt(2 x Rs 32,00,000 x Rs 25 / 0.10) = sqrt(Rs 1,60,00,00,000) = Rs 40,000.

q: The Baumol model of cash management is essentially based on the analogy that:

options.A: Cash should be managed in the same manner as fixed assets
options.B: Cash balances should always be kept equal to one month's expenditure
options.C: Surplus cash should be distributed as dividend immediately
options.D: Managing cash involves the same trade-off as managing inventory — a holding (opportunity) cost balanced against a transaction cost — so that the economic order quantity logic can be applied to cash

e: Baumol treats cash like inventory: holding cash carries an opportunity (interest) cost while each conversion of securities into cash carries a transaction cost, so the EOQ logic finds the balance minimising total cost.

q: Under the Miller-Orr model of cash management, an enterprise fixes a lower control limit of Rs 30,000 and a spread of Rs 90,000 between the control limits. The upper control limit is:
e: In Miller-Orr, upper limit = lower limit + spread = Rs 30,000 + Rs 90,000 = Rs 1,20,000. Cash reaching this limit triggers investment of the excess in securities.

q: In the Miller-Orr model of cash management, the spread between the control limits will be wider when:

options.A: The interest rate on marketable securities is higher
options.B: The cost of each transaction is very low
options.C: The variability (variance) of the daily cash flows is greater and the transaction cost is higher; it will be narrower when the interest rate is higher
options.D: The cash flows of the enterprise are perfectly steady and predictable

e: The spread grows with the variance of daily cash flows and with transaction cost, since wilder swings and costlier transfers need wider bands; a higher interest rate narrows it because idle cash is costlier.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 11,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 50,00,000. The Return on Investment of the division is:
e: Return on Investment = profit / capital employed x 100 = Rs 11,00,000 / Rs 50,00,000 x 100 = 22%.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 25,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 2,00,00,000. The cost of capital is 10%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = profit - cost of capital charge = Rs 25,00,000 - (10% x Rs 2,00,00,000) = Rs 25,00,000 - Rs 20,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) of a division is Rs 24,00,000, its capital employed is Rs 1,60,00,000 and the cost of capital is 10%. Its Economic Value Added (EVA) is:
e: EVA = NOPAT - (cost of capital x capital employed) = Rs 24,00,000 - (10% x Rs 1,60,00,000) = Rs 24,00,000 - Rs 16,00,000 = Rs 8,00,000.

q: Market Value Added (MVA) of an enterprise is measured as:

options.A: The net operating profit after tax minus the capital charge for the year
options.B: The book value of the total assets minus the total liabilities
options.C: The market value of the enterprise (the market value of its debt and equity together) minus the total capital invested in it
options.D: The sales of the enterprise minus its operating expenses

e: MVA is the excess of the total market value of the enterprise (debt plus equity) over the total capital investors have put into it; positive MVA means the firm has created wealth.

q: Which of the following measures belongs to the 'financial' perspective of the Balanced Scorecard?

options.A: Revenue growth rate and return on capital employed

e: Revenue growth and return on capital employed are financial outcomes, so they belong to the financial perspective; the other options relate to learning and growth, internal processes, and the customer perspective respectively.

q: A management audit is essentially concerned with appraising the 'three Es' of management, which stand for:
e: Management audit appraises how well management uses resources, judged by the three Es: Economy (least-cost inputs), Efficiency (input-output ratio) and Effectiveness (achievement of objectives).

q: In value engineering, a FAST (Function Analysis System Technique) diagram is used to:

options.A: Fix the selling price of the product
options.B: Depict the functions of a product and their logical inter-relationships (how and why each function is performed), so that costly or unnecessary functions can be identified and eliminated
options.C: Prepare the time schedule for the production of the product
options.D: Classify the stores items according to their annual consumption value

e: A FAST diagram arranges a product's functions in how-why logical order, showing which functions support which, so functions that cost more than their worth can be spotted and removed.

q: The expected market price of a product is Rs 1,500 per unit and the firm desires a profit margin of 25% on the selling price. The target cost of the product is:
e: Target cost = expected market price - desired profit = Rs 1,500 - (25% x Rs 1,500) = Rs 1,500 - Rs 375 = Rs 1,125 per unit.

q: Target costing can secure the largest reduction in the cost of a product when it is applied:

options.A: At the design and development stage of the product, where the bulk of its life-cycle costs are determined
options.B: After the production of the product has fully stabilised
options.C: At the time of preparation of the annual budget of the factory
options.D: In the marketing department, at the time of fixing the selling price

e: Most of a product's life-cycle cost is locked in at the design stage, before production begins; changes are cheapest then, so target costing applied at design and development secures the largest savings.

q: The actual cost of a product in the previous period was Rs 800 per unit. Under kaizen costing, a cost-reduction target of 5% is set for the current period. The kaizen target cost for the current period is:
e: Kaizen target cost = previous actual cost less the 5% reduction target = Rs 800 - (5% x Rs 800) = Rs 800 - Rs 40 = Rs 760 per unit.

q: Unlike traditional costing, life-cycle costing explicitly takes into account, as part of the total cost of a product or asset:

options.A: Only the direct material and direct labour costs
options.B: The end-of-life costs, such as decommissioning, dismantling, disposal and environmental restoration costs
options.C: Only the factory overheads of the first year
options.D: The selling expenses of the year of launch only

e: Life-cycle costing accumulates all costs over the product's whole life, including end-of-life costs like decommissioning, dismantling, disposal and environmental restoration, which traditional period costing overlooks.

q: A product gives a throughput of Rs 640 per unit and takes 0.4 hour of the bottleneck machine per unit. The return per factory (bottleneck) hour is:
e: Return per bottleneck hour = throughput per unit / bottleneck time per unit = Rs 640 / 0.4 hour = Rs 1,600 per factory hour.

q: In throughput accounting based on the Theory of Constraints, 'operating expense' means:

options.A: All the money spent by the system in converting inventory into throughput, that is, all costs other than the totally variable (material) cost, including labour, overheads and depreciation
options.B: Only the direct labour cost of the factory
options.C: The interest paid on the loans of the enterprise
options.D: The cost of goods sold computed under absorption costing

e: In throughput accounting, operating expense is all money spent converting inventory into throughput - every cost except totally variable material cost, including labour, overheads and even depreciation.

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 4,00,000 when the general price index stood at 110. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 165. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:
e: CPP restated value = historical cost x (current index / purchase index) = Rs 4,00,000 x 165 / 110 = Rs 6,00,000, expressing the asset in today's purchasing power.

q: The essential difference between the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method and the Current Cost Accounting (CCA) method of inflation accounting is that:

options.A: The CPP method is compulsory for all companies, whereas the CCA method is voluntary
options.B: The CPP method restates historical costs with the help of a general price index, in units of current purchasing power, whereas the CCA method uses the specific price changes, that is, the current replacement costs, of the particular assets
options.C: The CPP method deals only with fixed assets, whereas the CCA method deals only with stock
options.D: The CCA method ignores the effect of price changes altogether

e: CPP restates all items by one general price index, measuring changes in general purchasing power; CCA instead uses the specific current replacement cost of each asset, measuring changes in its own price.

q: The primary purpose of human resource accounting is to:

options.A: Fix the wages and salaries payable to the employees
options.B: Replace the payroll accounting system of the enterprise
options.C: Provide information about the cost and value of the human resources of the organisation, so that management can take better decisions regarding recruitment, training, deployment and retention of personnel
options.D: Value the employees of the enterprise for the purpose of selling them

e: Human resource accounting measures and reports the cost and value of people as organisational resources, helping management decide on recruitment, training, deployment and retention; it does not fix wages or value staff for sale.

q: Which of the following actions will, by itself, improve the Return on Investment of a division?

options.A: Increasing the capital employed, with no change in the profit earned
options.B: Increasing the operating costs of the division
options.C: Reducing the sales volume of the division
options.D: Reducing the investment in the assets employed, while maintaining the same profit

e: ROI = profit / capital employed. Reducing the investment in assets while keeping profit unchanged lowers the denominator, so ROI rises; the other options either raise capital or cut profit.

q: A large dam is being constructed for a client under a single agreement, the work being executed at the site over a period of three years. The method of costing most suitable for ascertaining the cost of this work is:
e: A single large work executed at site over a long period under one agreement is a contract, so contract costing - with a separate account for each contract - is the suitable method.

q: The total cost of producing 2,000 units is Rs 26,000 and that of producing 5,000 units is Rs 47,000. Using the high-low method, the variable cost per unit is:
e: Variable cost per unit = change in total cost / change in output = (Rs 47,000 - Rs 26,000) / (5,000 - 2,000) = Rs 21,000 / 3,000 = Rs 7 per unit.

q: Under GOLF analysis for selective control of inventory, stores items are classified on the basis of:

options.A: The source from which the items are procured — Government, Ordinary, Local or Foreign
options.B: The annual consumption value of the items
options.C: The rate at which the items are consumed
options.D: The unit price of the items

e: GOLF classifies items by source of supply: G for Government, O for Ordinary (trade), L for Local purchase and F for Foreign (imported), aiding procurement control.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 25,000 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 80 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 25,000 x 80 / 4) = sqrt(10,00,000) = 1,000 units, where annual ordering cost and annual carrying cost are equal.

q: 'Cost audit' primarily means:

options.A: Audit of the financial accounts of a company by a chartered accountant
options.B: Verification of the cost records and cost accounts to ensure that they are correctly maintained in accordance with the cost accounting principles and plan laid down
options.C: Audit of the stores and stock of a factory
options.D: Inspection of a factory by the Government for fixing prices

e: Cost audit verifies that cost records and accounts are correctly maintained according to the cost accounting principles and plan laid down; it is distinct from the financial audit and from stores inspection.
